newsitem.title: USA: U.S. seen handicapped in race for Asia gas market.
newsitem.headline: U.S. seen handicapped in race for Asia gas market.

text.p: U.S. producers are hobbling in the global competition to supply soaring Asian demand for natural gas because of U.S. taxes and policies, industry experts and government officials said Wednesday.
With world natural gas demand expected to explode to 145 trillion cubic feet by 2015, up 85 percent from 1995, big production projects are vying to supply those markets.

But industry consultants told a Senate panel Wednesday that U.S. natural gas exports would face tough competition in the Asian market because Middle Eastern and Asian countries with plentiful reserves were giving better terms than the United States for developing their fields.

"Oman and Qatar are willing to attract investors on the basis of fiscal systems that are more attractive than the United States ... and are capable of offering projects with a basic economic structure that is far superior over projects in the United States," Pedro van Meurs, a Calgary-based analyst, said in written testimony for the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee.
The committee held its first oversight hearing on natural gas in three years to discuss the state of the industry.

Committee chairman Frank Murkowski, an Alaska Republican, said he had a particular interest in the issue because his home state had 36 trillion cubic feet of gas reserves waiting to find an export market.

At the same time that Alaska is trying to sell its natural gas, officials said American companies looking to get into projects worldwide were up against foreign concerns that had strong government advocates pushing for them to win contracts.

"The governments of our major trade competitors are becoming increasingly aggressive and innovative in helping their firms secure major procurement in foreign markets," Deputy Assistant Energy Secretary David Jhirad said.
U.S. energy and finance agency officials said while they wanted all companies to compete on a level playing field, the real world was not that way yet.

"(U.S.) reserves are competitively disadvantaged largely because the government's not doing much to promote them," said a Senate aide, summarizing the outcome of the hearing. "The playing field is not level for U.S. companies."
